text: std::sort needs to know how to compare two elements, and writing a separate named function for every one-off comparison gets tedious fast. Lambdas — anonymous, inline functions — let you write that comparison exactly where you use it, often capturing variables from the surrounding scope. They're the glue between the containers and algorithms you've just learned and whatever custom logic your actual code needs.

A lambda is the square brackets, then parameters, then a body. The square brackets are the capture list, and they control which variables from the enclosing scope the lambda is even allowed to reach into.

Capturing a variable by value takes a snapshot — a copy, fixed at the moment the lambda is created. Capturing by reference instead captures an alias, so a later change to that variable is visible inside the lambda the next time it runs. It's worth naming your captures explicitly rather than reaching for the blanket capture-everything forms, because an explicit capture list documents exactly what the lambda depends on.

Most STL algorithms that need to know how to compare or test elements are built to accept a lambda directly. sort takes one here to reverse the usual ordering, and find_if takes one to locate the first element matching an arbitrary condition — no separate named function required for either.

auto is the right type when you're storing a lambda immediately in a local variable. But a lambda's actual type is unique and unnamed, so the moment you need to store it as a class member, pass it around, or swap in a different callable with the same signature, you reach for std::function instead. C++14 also lets a lambda's parameters be auto, letting one lambda work across several types, much like a template.

Lambdas let you write small, often-capturing functions exactly where an algorithm needs them, turning sort, find_if, and count_if into tools you customize on the spot. Next up, lesson twenty: choosing the right container — turning everything in this chapter into one decision framework.
